newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower as stocks and bonds fall.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower as stocks and bonds fall.

text.p: The dollar fell against most major currencies on the final trading day of the year, pressured by a sell-off in stocks and bonds.

Stock and bond prices tumbled after economic reports showed sales of new single-family homes rose at the fastest level in nearly four years in November and consumer confidence increased dramatically in December. Strong data hurt stocks and bonds because investors fear inflation may pick up if the economy overheats.
Although the dollar declined, traders played down the importance of the drop, which came in very light volume as foreign exchange trading wound down early before the New Year holiday Wednesday.
Financial markets in the United States and Europe will reopen Thursday, and trading in Japan will resume Monday.

"You have to keep in mind, too, that liquidity is so thin that this move is exaggerated," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International. "But essentially it was the stocks and bonds that got things started."
The price of the 30-year Treasury bond fell more than 1-1/4 points, while the Dow Jones industrial average slid more than 50 points in late trading.
The dollar had climbed to a fresh 45-month high of 116.40 Japanese yen in Europe before the surprisingly strong U.S. economic numbers hit the market.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 116.08 yen Tuesday, down from 116.15 yen Monday.
The dollar fell sharply to 1.5400 German marks from 1.5550 marks. The dollar's decline against the German currency was exacerbated by the mark's gains against the yen, according to traders.
The British pound soared Tuesday to $1.7163, its highest level in more than four years. In late trade, the pound settled at $1.7125, up from $1.6920 Monday.

The British currency gained amid expectations that interest rates in Britain are headed higher next year and as investors rushed to purchase pounds before the new year. Higher rates help the pound by making deposits denominated in that currency more attractive to investors.
In an interview with a French newspaper last week, Bank of England Gov. Eddie George said Britain may need to raise rates before the next general election to prevent the economy from overheating.
The pound's rise accelerated as pre-set orders to buy were triggered when the currency hit key levels, according to traders.
"There was clearly some year-end buying going on today that drove this thing higher in very thin markets," said Bob Near, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of New York.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.3400 Swiss francs from 1.3495 francs Monday, but rose slightly to Canadian $1.3705 from C$1.3697.
